Dada PSA, the PMC service desk

How to ask Dada IT for help, and how Dada IT works every request from the moment it arrives to the moment it is closed. Pick who you are and the guide shows the parts you need.

Start here

What Dada PSA is

Everyone

Dada PSA is where every IT request at PMC lives. It has two doors, one for the people who ask and one for the people who fix.

PMC RequestsFor every staff member. Raise a request, see where it has got to, add to it, approve a colleague's, and read the help articles. You see only your own requests.
The deskFor Dada IT. Every request lands on a board, gets a priority and running clocks, and is worked, noted, timed and closed there.

Signing in

  • Ward and office staff open PMC Requests through the Employee Portal, or at help.pmcne.ph. You sign in with your usual PMC account; there is no second password.
  • Dada IT opens the desk at desk.pmcne.ph and signs in with Microsoft (Entra), with the same MFA as email.

Never write a patient's details. Not in a request, a note, an email reply, an article or a file name. The ward, the room and the machine are all Dada IT ever needs. If a patient's details are written by mistake, the desk flags it for the author to tidy; it does not delete your words.

How a request travels

  1. It arrives. From PMC Requests, from an email to a board's address, from a phone call logged by Dada IT, or from a monitoring system.
  2. It lands on a board with a number (PMC-000123), a status of New, a company, a contact, and a priority worked out from two plain questions.
  3. The clocks start. Respond, Resolution plan and Resolve, each with a target for its priority.
  4. Someone owns it. A technician takes it, or the board's auto-assign gives it to someone. They write notes, book a visit if needed, and record their time.
  5. It is resolved and closed. The requester is told on PMC Requests (and by email if the board sends it), and is asked one question: how did we do?

Writing a good request

Say whereThe ward or office, the room, the machine's label. "Ward 3, room 302, the printer by the nurses' station."
Say since when"Since 7 this morning." It tells the technician whether it is new or has been building.
Say what you seeThe message on the screen, or the colour of the light. A photo of the screen helps most.
Leave the patient outNever a name, a case number or a bed-and-name. The desk does not need them to fix anything.
Asking for help

Follow and add to your request

Ward staff

Every request you raised is listed under Your requests, with where it has got to. Open one to read what Dada IT has told you and to add something.

  • Add a note or a photo at the foot of the request. It goes straight onto the ticket.
  • Reply to an email from the desk and your reply is added too. Keep the reference, for example [PMC-000123], in the subject.
  • If it is not fixed after it was closed, reply to the closing email. On most boards the request reopens; some boards open a new request instead.
  • Emails never carry the details. They say that something changed and link here; the words stay behind the sign-in.

How did we do?

When a request is closed, it asks you one question, with one to five stars and room for a sentence. It is asked once. Your answer goes to the service manager's reports.

Asking for help

Approve a request

Department approversManagers

Some requests need a yes before the work is done: a new account, access to a system, a purchase. If you approve for your department, they come to you.

  1. Open Approvals on PMC Requests, from the email or the top bar.
  2. Read the request and decide: Approve, or Decline. A decline must say why; an approval may add a note.
  3. That is all. Your decision goes on the ticket as a note the requester can read, and the ticket goes back to where it was. While it waited on you, its resolve clock was paused.

Only the approver can say yes. A technician cannot approve on your behalf.

Working the desk

The Service Board

TechniciansManagers

Every open ticket on the boards you are a member of, sorted worst clock first. Colour on the board means a clock, never decoration.

1

Reading the SLA chips

Each ticket carries up to three chips, one per clock. The number is time left, or how far past the target it is.

ChipMeans
R ✓Respond met: someone picked it up in time.
P 40mResolution plan due in 40 minutes. Amber is close.
S -2dResolve target passed by two days.
S pausedThe clock is stopped, because the ticket waits on a vendor, the requester or an approval.

Everyday moves

  • Take a ticket: open it and set yourself as Owner, or tick several rows and use the bulk bar.
  • Save a view: set the filters you use every morning and save them under a name.
  • Bulk actions: tick rows to change status, owner or board together, or attach them to a parent ticket.

When it cannot wait

Page the on-call sends the on-call person an email and a Teams card. It repeats every five minutes, up to three times, until they press Acknowledge on the ticket; then the duty manager is paged.

Working the desk

On your phone

Technicians

There is nothing to install. Open the desk in your phone's browser and it reshapes itself: the board becomes cards, and a ticket has Note, Ticket and Call at your thumb.

Your day

Schedule, Dispatch and In / out

TechniciansManagers

Schedule is the week by person. Dispatch is today. In / out is the board by the door: where everyone is right now.

  • Book a visit from the ticket's Schedule card or the form under the week. The desk warns you of a double booking; you may allow it on purpose.
  • Time off, a meeting or an activity goes in the same week, so nobody books you while you are away.
  • Dispatch shows today's visits and what is unassigned, for whoever hands out the work.

Say where you are

Your day

Calendar and your profile

TechniciansManagers

Your visits, time off, meetings and on-call shifts in one calendar, by day, week or month. Put it on your phone with a private feed.

  1. Open My profile from your name at the top right.
  2. Press Make a feed address. Copy the address it shows.
  3. Add it to your phone's calendar as a subscribed calendar. It names tickets and places, never what a ticket says. Making a new address stops the old one.
Your day

Time and timesheets

TechniciansManagers approve

Record time on the ticket as you work. Every entry lands in the week it was worked; at the end of the week you submit the week.

  1. On the ticket, add time: a start and end, or the hours. Choose the work role and work type; the board suggests them.
  2. On Timesheets, check the week against what you did, and press Submit.
  3. Your approver approves it, or rejects it with a reason. A rejected week opens again for you to fix and resubmit.

A submitted week takes no more time. If you forgot something, ask your approver to reopen it.

Knowing things

Knowledge base

TechniciansManagers

Write a fix once, use it again. An article is a title and the steps, for the desk only or for requesters too, in a category readers browse by.

  1. Write an article: the symptom, the cause, the steps, and how to check it worked.
  2. Say who it is for: the desk only, or the desk and requesters. Choose its board, its Subtype › Item and its category.
  3. Add pictures from its Files. A requester sees a picture only once it has been checked for patient details.
  4. Publish it. Requester articles appear on the Help page. Every save keeps the words it replaced.
  5. Link it to a ticket it helped with, from the ticket's Knowledge card.

Setting up

Setup at a glance

Administrators

Configuration lives in the desk, not in a deployment. A board's own settings take board admin; the rest take a system administrator. Every change is audited.

Boards and the service catalogue
A board is split by who does the work and how it flows. A service board takes incidents and requests; a change board runs assessment and approval; a project board has no SLA clocks. The catalogue is Type › Subtype › Item.
Members and security roles
Setup › Members lists everyone on the desk, with a page per person: boards and access, role, capacity, and deactivate when they leave, which takes them off every board and rota. A security role sets each module to None, Read, Write or Admin.
Workflow rules and recurring tickets
A rule is an event, conditions and actions: escalate, notify a person, a role or a Teams channel, or route. Test it, then switch it on. A recurring ticket raises a board template on a cadence.
Email connector
Which board claims which address, what never opens a ticket (an address, a domain, a subject phrase), and how the last week's mail was placed. Senders show by domain only; subjects are never shown.
Audit and API tokens
Every change the desk has written: who, when, what, and where from (the desk, the portal, the API, email, rules, BizBox). Filter and export. API tokens are minted here, shown once, one board and one scope each.
Calendars, schedule, time and departments
The working weeks the clocks run on and the holidays that stop them; visit statuses and locations; work roles and types; and which departments may raise to which board, with their approver.
Configuration types, knowledge categories, company status and type
The short lists: what a configuration can be and what each type asks; the categories readers browse knowledge by; and the words on a company.
Setting up

Setting up a board

Board administrators

A board's Setup page has a tab for each part of it: Board, Types, Statuses, SLA, Templates, Standard notes, Members & roles, Emails and Auto-assign.

What this board's emails say

Six kinds of email, each with a subject and a body in the board's own words. Four placeholders only: {ticket}, {board}, {actor} and {when}. There is no placeholder for the summary or a note, on purpose: an email leaves the building.

Who a new ticket goes to

A ticket that arrives with nobody named can be given an owner. A rule per Subtype › Item names the member; with no rule, the board's mode decides: nobody, the working member with the fewest open tickets, or the default team's leader.

A board that has set none of these behaves exactly as before: the desk's own email words, the survey on, and nobody auto-assigned.

Reference

Questions people ask

Everyone
I cannot see a request my colleague raised.
PMC Requests shows each person only their own requests. Ask your colleague, or ask Dada IT for its number.
My request is urgent but it shows P4.
Priority comes from who is affected and whether a patient is waiting. If the answers have changed, add a note saying so, or phone the desk. A technician can change the answers and the priority follows.
Why does the email not say what the technician wrote?
Because email leaves the hospital. The email tells you something changed; the words are on PMC Requests, behind your sign-in.
It was closed but it is still broken.
Reply to the closing email: on most boards it reopens, on some it opens a new request. Or raise a new request and mention the old number.
I am a technician and a board is missing from my board list.
Boards are membership only. Ask the board's administrator to add you on its Members & roles tab.
A restricted board: who sees it?
Only its members, and every read of its tickets is audited, including by a system administrator.
I forgot to enter time before I submitted my week.
Ask your approver to reopen the week, add the time, and submit again.
Can I delete a ticket or a note?
No. A duplicate is merged, a mistake is corrected with a new note, and an article is retired. History is kept.

Words the desk uses

Everyone
BoardA queue of work for one team, with its own statuses, clocks and members.
TicketOne request or incident, numbered PMC-000123.
RequesterThe person who asked. They see their own requests on PMC Requests.
OwnerThe technician working the ticket.
PriorityP1 to P4, from who is affected and whether a patient is waiting. Never typed.
SLA clocksRespond, Resolution plan and Resolve, each with a target for the priority, running on the board's working hours.
Subtype › ItemWhat the ticket is about, from the service catalogue: Printer › Failure.
Discussion noteA note the requester can read.
Internal noteA note for the desk only. Never sent, never shown to the requester.
Resolution noteHow it was fixed. The requester can read it.
ConfigurationA machine or device the desk looks after.
Restricted boardA board only its members see, with every read audited.
PageAn urgent call to the on-call, repeated until acknowledged.
TimesheetYour week of time entries, submitted and approved.
In / outWhere each member is right now, said by themselves.
UpliftThe evidence of the service's hours and work by commercial classification.
